slides.text:
A `switch` compares one value against several cases and runs the first one that matches. It replaces a long `else if` chain. In Go a case ends by itself, with no `break`.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
look at a value
    if it is A, do this
    if it is B or C, do that
    if nothing matches, do the other

slides.text:
Two sessions:

- **Session 1:** cases on a value, lists of values, a switch with no value and `fallthrough`
- **Session 2:** a setup statement, `break` inside a case and the order of the cases

exercises.title: Switch on a value
exercises.guide: Pick a path by comparing one value against several cases.

chunks.guide: `switch` compares `day` with each `case`, from the top. The first match runs its block and the switch ends. `default` runs when nothing matches.

notes.text: Compares day with each case below.

chunks.text:
switch day {
    case 1:
        fmt.Println("Monday")
    case 2:
        fmt.Println("Tuesday")
    case 3:
        fmt.Println("Wednesday")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Another day")
    }

chunks.guide: This line runs after the switch.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: Only the matching case runs, and the switch ends there. Go never continues into the next case on its own.

exercises.title: Several values in a case
exercises.guide: Let one case match a list of values.

chunks.guide: A `case` can list values separated by commas. It matches when the switched value equals any of them.

notes.text: One match is enough to run the block.

chunks.text:
switch letter {
    case "a", "e", "i", "o", "u":
        fmt.Println("vowel")
    case "y":
        fmt.Println("sometimes")
    default:
        fmt.Println("consonant")
    }

exercises.title: Why does it not compile?
exercises.guide: Read the message, then pick the cause.
exercises.code:
./main.go:9:7: invalid case "two" in
  switch on n (mismatched types
  untyped string and int)
options: Strings cannot be used in a `case`
A `case` value must match the type of the switch
Each `case` needs a `break` to end it
exercises.explanation: Every case is compared with the switched value, so it must have the same type. `n` is an `int`, and `"two"` is a string.

exercises.title: Switch with no value
exercises.guide: Drop the value after `switch` and write a condition in each case.

chunks.guide: With no value, each `case` holds a `bool` condition. The first true one runs, like an `else if` chain that reads flatter.

notes.text: Nothing to compare: the cases are conditions.

chunks.text:
switch {
    case hour < 12:
        fmt.Println("morning")
    case hour < 18:
        fmt.Println("afternoon")
    default:
        fmt.Println("evening")
    }

exercises.title: Catch the rest
exercises.guide: Run the last branch when no case matches.

exercises.title: Fall through
exercises.guide: Ask a case to continue into the next one with `fallthrough`.

chunks.guide: `fallthrough` runs the block of the next case too, without checking its value. It must be the last statement of its case.

notes.text: Jumps into the next case, whatever its value.

chunks.text:
switch stars {
    case 2:
        fmt.Println("good")
        fallthrough
    case 1:
        fmt.Println("rated")
    default:
        fmt.Println("none")
    }

slides.text:
Like `if`, a `switch` can start with a short statement, then a `;`. The variable it declares exists only inside the switch, and it can be the value that the cases compare.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
A `break` inside a case ends the switch early, which helps when a case has a check halfway through. Cases are tried from the top, and `default` runs last wherever it is written.

exercises.title: Switch with a setup
exercises.guide: Declare a value in the switch line and compare it.

chunks.guide: The part before the `;` runs first. `size` lives only inside this switch, and the part after the `;` is the value to compare.

notes.text: After the setup, this is the value to compare.

chunks.text:
switch size := len("go"); size {
    case 1:
        fmt.Println("single")
    case 2:
        fmt.Println("pair")
    default:
        fmt.Println("long")
    }

chunks.guide: This line runs after the switch.

exercises.title: Setup and conditions
exercises.guide: Combine a setup with cases that hold conditions.

chunks.guide: With a setup and no value, the `;` stays and each `case` holds a condition that can use the new variable.

notes.text: An expression works as the setup.
Nothing to compare after the setup: cases are conditions.

chunks.text:
switch n := 7 * 2; {
    case n > 20:
        fmt.Println("large")
    case n > 10:
        fmt.Println("medium")
    default:
        fmt.Println("small")
    }

chunks.guide: This line runs after the switch.

exercises.title: Complete the switch
exercises.guide: Compare the value from the setup, and catch every other value.

exercises.title: Leave a case early
exercises.guide: Use `break` to end the switch before the case finishes.

chunks.guide: `break` jumps out of the switch at once, so the lines left in the case are skipped.

notes.text: Ends the whole switch, not just the if.

chunks.guide: This line runs after the switch.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `default` runs only when no case matches, wherever it is written. The first true case, `x > 3`, runs and ends the switch.
